items.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun

HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). items.title: Import AI 475: Swarm scaling; Google DeepMind watermarks biology; and the AI science economy
items.raw_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry: …How does swarm scaling work?… Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time. “Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes. What they found: “18,000 posts from autonomous AI agents (self-identifying as from OpenAI) using the public internet to communicate during a web-retrieval task”. The researchers think this is because the agents were given a web-lookup task. “As part of the task, they were supposed to have the ability to read the internet but not to write on it. They found a way to use their read access to write information to an obscure German wiki,” the researchers write. “The agents used this wiki to communicate information with each other, primarily to help them succeed at their task. They asked for answers, pooled results, and shared techniques for bypassing their restrictions. This allowed them to use the work of others to cheat on their task… OpenAI found out about this. items.title: COP31 ends in failure as countries split over fossil fuels, climate finance
items.raw_text: ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams. As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism. Many countries were not buying it. Read full article Comments

items.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair
items.raw_text: Nvidia's board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is "effective immediately" and was based in part on "input from senior levels of the United States government" that assured the board members that "Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk." That assurance comes despite Huang's admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. items.title: F1 in Las Vegas: You've never seen an F1 race like this before
items.raw_text: Las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023 , the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing. The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very quickly , leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor. But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle . Read full article Comments

items.title: Tri-screen portable monitors aren’t for the faint of heart

I’ve experimented with dual-screen laptops in multiple form factors and numerous portable monitors, including ones with projection capabilities . items.title: Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI
items.raw_text: Buying a new computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense . Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia's new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models. While it doesn't have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16 , with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you're looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error. The PC stuff Before we dive into the AI agents, let's talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia's pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn't skimp on the specs. Read full article Comments

items.title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
items.raw_text: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land. The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access. With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses. items.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
items.raw_text: It's a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki's sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most. (Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We'll give you a heads-up when we get there.) As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945. items.title: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
items.raw_text: At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US). These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements. These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “ race science ” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas , recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism. Read full article Comments

items.title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
items.raw_text: The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state's right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations. AT&T's status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027. The order released today granted AT&T's request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC's previous approval of AT&T's petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California's rules in July. Read full article Comments

items.title: SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business
items.raw_text: The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine. "SpaceX's potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX," Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday. CNN first reported the letter's existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor. items.title: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
items.raw_text: Google's flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that has been in testing for the past few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image-generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that sat next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. However, it wasn't in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search. Read full article Comments

items.title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
items.raw_text: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
items.raw_text: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. items.title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
items.raw_text: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act. In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.” Shared envelopes Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges. Read full article Comments

items.title: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain
items.raw_text: SpaceX's successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA's path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year. For SpaceX's purposes, Saturday's mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX's deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon. Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX's existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship. Read full article Comments

items.title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
items.raw_text: The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons. Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing : The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts. CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications." items.title: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger
items.raw_text: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week. The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week. "Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday . "Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information." Read full article Comments

items.title: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
items.raw_text: When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn't secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change. "We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels," Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained." If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025 , with additional price hikes happening this year. Read full article Comments

items.title: US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop
items.raw_text: The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA's effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved. The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic. Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN . Bedford also said that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20. Read full article Comments

items.title: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space
items.raw_text: Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers. The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips. SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter. items.title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
items.raw_text: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil. But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods. items.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
items.raw_text: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. items.raw_text: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. items.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
items.raw_text: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering. The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste. In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System. “Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says. Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks. Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted. items.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
items.raw_text: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US. Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time. This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics. Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry. We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
items.raw_text: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

items.raw_text: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.raw_text: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.raw_text: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.raw_text: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.raw_text: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

items.raw_text: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap , the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub .) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can visit this link to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly. items.title: datasette 1.0a43
items.raw_text: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-

items.title: datasette-apps 0.4a0
items.raw_text: Release: datasette-apps 0.4a0 Datasette Apps are sandboxed HTML and JavaScript applications that live inside Datasette - think Claude Artifacts, but these ones can run SQL queries against your data. 0.4a0 adds support for linking: you can link to an app with #fragments in the URL and the app can see and use those, plus supported URL schemes are reported back to Datasette Agent so it can help write apps that link to each other. This means you can have e.g. an app that shows details about a specific record, and a completely separate app that searches those records and links to their representations in the first app. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette-apps , datasette , urls

items.title: datasette-llm 0.1a11
items.raw_text: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0 ) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model ' { "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" } ' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model! items.raw_text: Release: datasette-cluster-map 0.19 One of the oldest Datasette plugins, and still one of my favorites. It now works with Datasette 1.0a42, and depends on the new datasette-leaflet to ensure OpenStreetMap tiles are requested with a referrer header. items.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
items.raw_text: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

items.raw_text: We are starting a non-profit research organization: STABL . Adapting to advanced AI will require dramatic institutional change and broad societal resilience. It will also require evidence about AI progress and impacts — the prospects of recursive self-improvement (RSI), the pace of AI diffusion, and the bottlenecks that constrain how AI capabilities translate into societal outcomes. Four theses define our worldview: We consider advanced AI a transformative general-purpose technology with the potential for broad societal benefits. Yet we recognize that the pace of societal transformation will be bottlenecked by the speed of human and organizational change more than progress in capabilities. Our institutions — the established ways we organize knowledge, work, and governance — are an important source of stability during this turbulent period, but they also need serious reforms to keep serving their purpose. We favor a broad portfolio of defenses to manage AI risks, of which alignment is only one part. Resilience, the most neglected component today, must become central. Another way to state our worldview is to place it on a 2x2 chart. The vertical axis depicts taking AI’s transformative potential seriously. The horizontal axis depicts taking downstream bottlenecks to AI’s impacts seriously. items.raw_text: By Felix Chen, Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, and Arvind Narayanan. See the full author list and affiliations here . There are growing calls for independent and embedded AI evaluation, especially of AI agents. But much remains unclear: what constitutes a “good” evaluation, what needs to be evaluated in the first place, and how best to coordinate and support the influx of people entering the burgeoning evaluation ecosystem. Our group at Princeton has been working to improve the state of AI agent evaluation for about three years . We teamed up with people who’ve done foundational work on evaluation at Stanford, the UK AI Security Institute, and Brookings. Our paper is titled Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation. We synthesized the trends we see across three dimensions—the science and methods, the research agenda, and the evaluation ecosystem—with the goal to help those who are upskilling for this new paradigm. We also aim to equip evaluators, funders, and the public with a set of questions to ask, and provide actionable recommendations. Thirty-three emerging trends in AI agent evaluation. items.title: Steering AI Beyond Automation
items.raw_text: By Gabriel Unger and Arvind Narayanan. Unger is an economist at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. One of the most fundamental questions for the field of AI today is: to what extent is the project of AI purely about automating human labor? The dominant Silicon Valley program for AI right now, with both industry and academic faces, answers: “almost entirely.” 1 There is an implicit technological determinism: that AI has a deep internal logic that favors automation. To keep pushing in this direction is to move towards economic growth, prosperity, and profit. The vision of AGI is the successful completion of this project: to create AI systems capable enough to autonomously do everything a human can do. There is an alternative view : that AI is a technology (or class of technologies) that, like any technology, can develop in different directions. Total automation is one direction. But there are others, including directions that focus more on human augmentation, and increasing the collaborative and collective power of teams of humans and AI models working together. This view — our view — is not that automation is never good. Clearly sometimes it is, and clearly sometimes some subset of people try to oppose it out of the narrowest short-term self interest, at the expense of broader social and economic progress. But we think AI can also augment human workers in many interesting ways, that some of the maximalist attempts to completely automate all human labor are deeply unpromising on b

items.title: A big-tent or small-tent AI safety movement?
items.raw_text: In recent weeks, two narratives about AI safety have emerged: either AI existential risk is real and imminent, or AI leaders’ and whistleblowers’ claims to that effect are insincere — a “psyop” or hype or a twisted form of regulatory capture. Few have considered the third possibility that x-risk warnings are sincere but simply wrong and counterproductive to AI safety . It’s as if everyone takes for granted that those raising the alarm are geniuses, and the only question is whether they’re the benevolent or the evil kind of genius. We subscribe to neither narrative. In our writing on AI safety , we’ve consistently tried to take the arguments seriously but rebut the many claims we think are unsound while highlighting safety concerns that we think are real. This essay is a continuation of that agenda. It is true that we systematically underinvest in resilience against catastrophic and systemic risks Let’s start by steelmanning a subset of AI safety and Effective Altruist (EA) arguments. Something is deeply wrong in the world when it comes to how much we invest in defending against catastrophic risks, and the safety and EA communities are right about that. Take superintelligence out of the equation entirely and it remains true that evidence-grounded risk arguments have been made for years and not produced a commensurate policy response. The most well known example is the failure to prepare for pandemics. We had years of warnings and quantitative estimates. A 2019 report convened

items.title: AI existential risk probabilities are (still) too unreliable to inform policy
items.raw_text: Over two years ago we wrote a detailed deconstruction of p(doom) and argued that its primary effect is to launder vague intuitions and fears through a facade of quantification. The essay has fresh relevance today as p(doom) rhetoric is driving public discourse and policy attention to an unprecedented degree. Unsurprisingly, today’s probability estimates of AI existential risk are no more rigorous than the ones from 2024. Hence this repost. We should be clear about what we’re not saying. We aren’t saying forecasters (or others who attempt to quantify AI x-risk) intend to mislead. Unfortunately, we think the effect is misleading nonetheless. In general, being quantitative about forecasts is good. In fact, Arvind has been serving as an advisor to the Forecasting Research Institute’s Longitudinal Expert AI Panel , an effort he thinks is extremely valuable. As the essay makes clear, the infeasibility of building useful quantitative models is specific to forecasts of AI x-risk, not forecasting in general. Our goal here is not to try to push AI safety advocates to stop communicating in terms of probabilities (not that we’d succeed even if we tried). Rather, our hope in publishing this is for those at the receiving end of these probabilities — especially policymakers — to recognize that unlike almost every other quantitative forecast that we encounter, they are not the result of a validated model or method. items.raw_text: This essay is over 13,000 words long and represents our most substantial writing on AI safety since the original essay. Over the last few months, loss - of - control incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic have intensified concerns about AI safety. Warnings about existential risk have increasingly reached the broader public, alongside calls to slow AI development. Dario Amodei’s call to “ pace the frontier ” reflects the concern that safety efforts are not keeping up with AI capabilities. The most prominent example was the OpenAI - Hugging Face incident , where hundreds of OpenAI agents got access to the internet and hacked Hugging Face to find how they were being graded on an evaluation. Over the last two weeks, the details of many other instances of such activity from OpenAI agents being evaluated have surfaced, such as agents using an old Wiki website to communicate with each other despite restrictions on such activity, or attacking a software repository to attempt to upload malicious software. The AI safety community has viewed these incidents largely as a crisis for alignment . 1 In this view, alignment will become harder over time as agents learn to reason covertly, and as a result, loss-of-control incidents are likely to become much more widespread and damaging as agents become more capable. items.title: AI agents can't yet do open-ended AI research
items.raw_text: The goal of leading AI labs is recursive self-improvement (RSI): the automation of AI research using AI agents. RSI also underpins forecasts of explosive AI progress. How can we assess if we are close to this milestone? One way is to use benchmarks that test if agents can conduct AI research. Given the AI community’s focus on benchmarks, they have been the dominant way to evaluate progress towards RSI. Over the last year, many such evaluations have found that agents are now able to make progress on tasks where success is easily verifiable, prompting speculation that we are on the verge of RSI. But while these evaluations are helpful, they are limited to narrow, verifiable tasks. AI research can be much more open-ended. Success is often not immediately clear or verifiable, and to make progress, researchers need to test promising hypotheses, backtrack, or consider new or unconventional approaches. How can we evaluate agents’ ability to conduct open-ended AI research? We take our first step towards answering this question in a new paper . We partnered with the authors of two unpublished AI papers and asked them to draft their papers’ main research questions. We then tasked frontier AI agents with conducting research to answer these questions, and gave them thousands of dollars of API credits and compute, and six days of wall-clock time. items.title: What will be left for us to work on?
items.raw_text: I had the honor of giving a keynote at the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul last week titled “What will be left for us to work on?” I addressed the widespread anxiety about how we should adapt as AI capabilities increase. I was thrilled by the talk’s reception, so I have made my slides available here , annotated with a lightly edited transcript. You can also view them below right here on this page, but the online version has animations, clickable links, and a much nicer experience overall. Update [August 2026]: ICML has released the video of the talk. I made three arguments. First, the AI as Normal Technology framework is a correct and useful as a way to think about AI’s impacts, unless and until there is some future discontinuity such as through recursive self-improvement. Second, even though we should take recursive self-improvement seriously, there is no milestone that companies might achieve in the lab that will suddenly put us all out of work. Third and finally, jobs of the future will be radically different, and a lot of adaptation will be needed. I shared my thinking about what this might look like and ended with a vision of human/AI “co-superintelligence”. Now is a time of great excitement in AI, but it’s also a time of great anxiety in the AI community. I want to address that anxiety head on. items.raw_text: By Arvind Narayanan and Akash Kapur Our goal in this essay is to move beyond the debate over whether AI is a bubble. We do so in two ways: clearly separating current financials from the question of who captures value in the long run, and recognizing that the labs are not confined to be model providers. They can migrate up the stack and are already aggressively doing so. This will likely allow them to escape the commodity trap but raises new concerns — customer lock-in and reduced competition. Akash Kapur is a visiting fellow at Princeton and a senior fellow at New America. He is no relation to Sayash Kapoor. As leading AI companies continue to invest massively in capacity and race toward blockbuster IPOs, serious questions linger about their business models. How will these companies — along with the vast ecosystem of chipmakers, hyperscalers, and infrastructure partners that depends on them — recoup the estimated $4–8 trillion projected to be invested in AI infrastructure by the early 2030s? The current conversation splits between critics and boosters. Critics point to mounting losses, the gap between capex and revenue, and reports about the leading labs’ massive cash burn. Boosters cite accelerating rapid revenue growth, enterprise adoption, and milestones like Anthropic’s first profitable quarter . Each camp has a valid point. items.title: Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t
items.raw_text: There is great anxiety and uncertainty about AI replacing jobs. How can we move past vague warnings and bombastic predictions and bring data to bear on this question? One good way is to look at the profession where AI capabilities are furthest along and adoption has been exceptionally rapid: software engineering. In this essay, we argue that there is enough evidence to reject the narrative that once AI capabilities reach a certain threshold, it will cause mass layoffs. Given that this is true even in a sector with very few regulatory barriers, most other professions are likely to be even more cushioned. We also have a good understanding of why this is the case. We can think of many kinds of knowledge work, including software development, as a “decide-execute-deliver sandwich”. AI compresses the “execute” layer — the middle of the sandwich — but the other two layers resist automation in a way that will not be overcome by capability improvements alone. We conclude on a note of cautious optimism about the future trajectory of demand for software engineering. This essay is the first in a series, and the next one will look at reasons why individual software engineers’ careers might be rocky even if overall demand is healthy. items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Rishi Bommasani, Andrew Schwartz, Arvind Narayanan At Google’s developer conference earlier this week, the company launched its latest model, Gemini 3.5 Flash, alongside a new agent app, Antigravity 2.0. To showcase what this new agent setup is capable of, Google claimed that a team of agents had built an entire operating system. The effort reportedly required only a single prompt, cost only about $900 in API fees, and was carried out by a few dozen subagents working together. Does this mean that complex pieces of software can now be built cheaply by AI? Not so fast: The “single prompt” claim is misleading. The blog post says the operating system was built from a single prompt. But halfway through the post, Google discloses that the prompt “ended up being many thousands of lines” long. How many attempts did it take to generate the prompt? How specific were the instructions to the agent? Without these critical details, it is hard to know if the secret sauce is a better model or just more effort put into prompting the model. Moreover, the run was carried out on a scaffold 1 with specialized roles, delegation to subagents, and an agent to detect and prevent cheating. In the launch post, Google views the scaffold as a product feature. But we don’t know whether the scaffold was overfit to this task of building an operating system from scratch, or whether it would perform as well on other complex software engineering tasks. items.title: Do AI Risks Require Extraordinary Government Intervention?
items.raw_text: In a recent essay, Derek Thompson engages with AI as Normal Technology (AINT). He agrees with our thesis about AI’s slow labor market impacts, relying on the fact that GDP growth has so far been average, unemployment is below 5%, and even jobs that seemed vulnerable to automation show rising employment and wages. He concludes that so far, the macroeconomic picture is consistent with what we would expect from a “normal” general-purpose technology. But when it comes to AI risks, he is far more bearish. He points to examples of cyber- and bio-risks and expresses pessimism about AI quickly becoming dangerous across many new domains. He argues that AI’s emergent capabilities make it fundamentally different from previous technologies, and that this difference justifies “extraordinary” government responses including restrictions on what companies can release. 1 In this essay, we lay out the downsides of extraordinary government intervention in response to new technology. We discuss proposals for improving resilience that do not require such intervention. We also discuss why governments have so far been reluctant to invest in resilience. In short, resilience requires us to get better at the *normal* process of policymaking. But sclerosis in the federal government and the ease of justifying interventions on AI companies rather than society at large make extraordinary intervention seem appealing, despite its limitations. items.raw_text: This post is 8,000 words long—it is our new collaborative paper on an emerging type of AI evaluation. The paper is also published in a PDF format here . Summary : AI models have started to saturate most major benchmarks. But does that mean they can build and ship a real product, or conduct a scientific experiment end-to-end, or navigate a government bureaucracy? Researchers have started testing AI in such real-world settings. We call these evals “open-world evaluations”. This essay defines open-world evaluations, surveys the lessons learned so far, and lays out best practices for conducting them. We also introduce CRUX, a collaboration of 17 researchers from academia, government, civil society, and industry that will regularly evaluate frontier AI capabilities through open-world evaluations. In our first experiment, an AI agent built and published an iOS app to the App Store, making just two errors, one of which required manual intervention. This gives us an early indication of potentially useful capabilities and, more importantly, an early warning about the potential for AI-driven app store spam (we disclosed this result to Apple a month before publication). We hope to conduct similar experiments to surface early warnings across other real-world domains; this will be one of our main empirical projects over the coming year. items.title: New Paper: Towards a science of AI agent reliability
items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan Suppose you hear about a new AI agent for improving productivity — by making purchases, or writing code, or sending emails, or handling a customer on your behalf. Should you trust it? Can the agent do the job reliably enough? After all, there are many horror stories of agents going wrong. Surprisingly, even though the lack of reliability of AI agents is well known, right now the AI industry doesn’t have good tools for measuring reliability, or even a good definition of reliability. Arvind and Sayash have long been thinking about this. Last fall, we were joined by postdoctoral researcher Stephan Rabanser , whose PhD looked at the reliability question in simpler, more traditional AI systems. We recruited a few other independent researchers, and have released what we hope is a comprehensive measurement of reliability. Our draft paper is called Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability . We borrowed insights from many other fields, such as nuclear and aviation safety. We were able to decompose reliability into 12 different dimensions. Evaluating 14 models on two complementary benchmarks, we found that nearly two years of rapid capability progress have produced only modest reliability gains. See our interactive dashboard here . items.raw_text: Microsoft 365 kampt sinds gistermiddag 17.15 uur Nederlandse tijd met een wereldwijde storing. Verschillende diensten, waaronder Outlook en Microsoft Teams, zijn hierdoor moeilijk bereikbaar of werken helemaal niet. Gebruikers hebben problemen met hun e-mail en kunnen niet online vergaderen. Ook AI-functies van Copilot werken niet. Volgens Microsoft komt de storing door een "verhoogde belasting" van de infrastructuur. Op X schrijft Microsoft dat dit komt doordat "een aantal servers onverwacht niet beschikbaar is, waardoor de resterende infrastructuur onder druk komt te staan". Van een cyberaanval is volgens het techbedrijf geen sprake. Wat dan wel de oorzaak van de storing is, maakt het bedrijf naar eigen zeggen pas bekend zodra het probleem is verholpen. De storing is voor zover bekend merkbaar in ruim zeventig landen. Herstart nog niet gelukt Microsoft zegt "met man en macht" te werken aan een oplossing. Zo wordt geprobeerd de getroffen systemen te herstarten. Vannacht meldde het bedrijf dat pogingen hiertoe nog niet het gewenste effect hadden. In de vroege ochtend meldde het techbedrijf dat diensten deels weer zouden moeten werken. Rond 08.45 uur sprak Microsoft van "positieve resultaten en verhoogde capaciteit", maar er is nog altijd geen stabiele oplossing. Wereldwijd zijn er meer dan 430 miljoen gebruikers van Microsoft 365, een abonnement waarin Office-apps als Word, Excel en Powerpoint zitten. items.title: FBI: Noord-Korea gebruikte deepfakes om honderden miljoenen aan crypto te stelen
items.raw_text: Noord-Koreaanse hackers hebben volgens de FBI met slinkse deepfakevideo's in anderhalf jaar tijd zo'n 400 miljoen dollar in crypto buit weten te maken, meer dan 350 miljoen euro. De Amerikaanse politiedienst vond meer dan 900 deepfakevideo's van slachtoffers, die gebruikt werden om nieuwe mensen te duperen. De hackers deden zich voor als een bekende van hun slachtoffers. Ze benaderden die met een boodschap om met een videobelletje weer eens bij te kletsen of een samenwerking te bespreken. Slachtoffers hadden niet door dat de videobeelden van deze persoon waren gemaakt met AI. Het videogesprek verliep ook niet via bekende apps als Zoom, Teams of Meets, maar via niet van echt te onderscheiden kopieën daarvan, die draaien op Noord-Koreaanse servers. Slachtoffers kregen tijdens de gesprekken een bericht dat er iets mis was met hun verbinding, wat ze zogenaamd konden verhelpen via een link die werd meegestuurd. Maandenlang geduld Wie op de link klikte, werd digitaal overgeleverd aan de hackers. Die kregen toegang tot cryptoaccounts, mailgegevens en chatberichten. Ook werden opnames via de webcam gemaakt, om bekenden van het slachtoffer te benaderen met diens gezicht. Omdat de hackers ook communicatie in handen hadden, konden ze zich in berichten makkelijk voordoen als het slachtoffer, zeker als ze ook diens accounts op LinkedIn, Telegram, Slack of Discord hadden overgenomen. items.title: Topman Huang van chipbedrijf Nvidia vertrekt per direct vanwege affaires
items.raw_text: Het doek is gevallen voor Jensen Huang als topman van chipbedrijf Nvidia. De CFO, de huidige financiële topvrouw Colette Kress, neemt de functie tijdelijk over. Het bedrijf is daarnaast een zoektocht gestart naar een opvolger. Daarvoor wordt binnen en buiten het bedrijf gekeken. Huang was in 1993 een van de oprichters van Nvidia, dat qua beurswaarde een van de waardevolste bedrijven ter wereld is. Hij heeft een sleutelrol gespeeld in het succes van het bedrijf. Het zou gaan om Kimberly Powell, vicepresident gezondheidszorg bij het concern. De krant baseert zich op anonieme bronnen binnen het bedrijf. Powell heeft het bericht nog niet bevestigd. De onthulling kwam enkele dagen na het nieuws dat Huang een affaire had met Alice Huang. Zij is leidinggevende bij Megaspeed, een Singaporese klant van de Amerikaanse chipmaker, en wordt ervan verdacht voor China te spioneren. items.title: Een zwarte leren jas en AI-visionair: wie is Nvidia-topman Jensen Huang?
items.raw_text: "Ik heb er heel veel van, wel dertig of veertig", zei Nvidia-oprichter en topman Jensen Huang over zijn kenmerkende zwarte jas tegen CBS News . Elke dag draagt hij hetzelfde, zodat hij zich naar eigen zeggen op andere zaken kan richten. Het grootste deel van die jassen kreeg hij van zijn vrouw Lori. Over die echtgenote heeft Huang gisteren toegegeven dat hij haar heeft bedrogen, mogelijk met een Chinese spionne. De affaire veroorzaakte veel opschudding en leidde tot een ongekende koersval vandaag op de beurs van New York. 'Koppige ondernemer' De topman blijft voorlopig leidinggeven aan het chipbedrijf, dat hij zelf oprichtte in 1993. Dat deed hij niet in een garage, zoals de oprichters van Apple of Google, maar met twee collega's in de Amerikaanse restaurantketen Denny's. Het werd een van de waardevolste bedrijven ter wereld. In de biografie The Thinking Machine beschrijft auteur Stephen Witt het als het verhaal van een "koppige ondernemer" die zijn visie doorzette en daarmee een van de rijkste mannen ter wereld werd: Huang staat op plek 10 van de Bloomberg Billionare Index, met een geschat fortuin van 155 miljard dollar. Van Taiwan naar Silicon Valley Jen-Hsun Huang, later verengelst naar Jensen, werd in 1963 geboren in Taiwan. Zijn ouders verkochten veel van hun bezittingen om hem op jonge leeftijd naar familie in de Verenigde Staten te kunnen sturen. items.title: Huang terug als ceo van Nvidia na onderzoek naar veiligheidsrisico’s
items.raw_text: Chipontwerper Nvidia heeft Jensen Huang met onmiddellijke ingang herbenoemd tot president, ceo en lid van de raad van bestuur. De raad van bestuur stemde unaniem in met zijn terugkeer na gesprekken met Huang en overleg met de Amerikaanse overheid. Volgens het bedrijf ziet de raad geen risico’s voor de nationale veiligheid. Dat staat in een persverklaring die het bedrijf voorbeurs bekendmaakte. Huang keert terug nadat Nvidia eerder een onafhankelijk onderzoek was gestart. Dat gebeurde na berichtgeving dat hij doelwit zou zijn geweest van een buitenlandse inlichtingenoperatie . Toen ook bekend werd dat Huang er binnen het bedrijf er een relatie op nahield moest hij het veld ruimen . Voor dat onderzoek stelde de raad een speciale commissie van onafhankelijke bestuurders aan, ondersteund door externe juridische adviseurs. Jones stelt dat de raad ervan overtuigd is dat Huang de juiste persoon is om Nvidia te leiden. Tijdens zijn afwezigheid werd de functie waargenomen door Colette Kress, die daarnaast financieel directeur van het bedrijf blijft. Ook zou personeel gedreigd hebben om op te stappen als Huang niet terugkeerde. items.title: ‘Ai-agents laten opvallend veel sporen na bij cyberaanval’
items.raw_text: Interview met Northwave-directeur Pim Takkenberg Cybercriminelen zetten ai steeds vaker in om aanvallen te versnellen en op te schalen. Toch blijken diezelfde ai-systemen soms meer sporen achter te laten dan traditionele aanvallers doen. Directeur van cyberbeveiliger Northwave, Pim Takkenberg, ziet daarin kansen voor verdedigers, maar waarschuwt ook voor nieuwe risico’s zoals deepfakes en beveiligings-incidenten door ongecontroleerd gebruik van ai-toepassingen binnen organisaties. Cybercriminelen die kunstmatige intelligentie inzetten, kunnen aanvallen veel sneller uitvoeren dan voorheen. Ze genereren in hoog tempo nieuwe scripts, testen meerdere aanvalspaden tegelijk en werken dag en nacht door. Toch zijn ze niet onaantastbaar. Soms laten ai-agents juist meer sporen achter dan een menselijke aanvaller ooit zou doen. Dat zegt Northwave-directeur Pim Takkenberg in een uitgebreid gesprek met Computable over de invloed van ai op cybersecurity. Takkenberg schuift regelmatig aan bij actualiteitenprogramma’s als Nieuwsuur om in een paar minuten op tv cyberincidenten te duiden. Vanuit het hoofdkantoor van Northwave op bedrijventerrein Papendorp in Utrecht kijkt hij er deze keer naar uit om wat langer de tijd te nemen voor een inhoudelijk gesprek met ict-vakblad Computable. Om de impact van ai op cyberaanvallen te illustreren haalt hij een incident bij een klant aan. items.title: Kort: Ai-tokens zetten ict onder druk, kritieke lekken in F5 Big-IP en meer
items.raw_text: In het nieuwsoverzicht van Computable: explosieve groei ai-tokens legt druk op opslag- en infrastructuursystemen, 5 kritieke kwetsbaarheden in F5 BIG-IP, een nieuwe beheerlaag van SoftwareOne voor Claude binnen AWS, Nederlands startkapitaal voor ai-platform cannabisinformatie Toke en cybersecuritybedrijf Northwave wint innovatieprijs. Explosieve groei ai-tokens zet druk op infrastructuur en opslag De snelle opmars van kunstmatige intelligentie vraagt de komende jaren om fors meer rekenkracht, geheugen en opslagcapaciteit. Dat blijkt uit het rapport Tokenomics 2030 van Sandisk. Volgens het model kan de wereldwijde productie van ai-tokens stijgen van circa vijf miljard per seconde in 2026 naar 317 miljard per seconde in 2030. Dat betekent dat ai-systemen over vier jaar ruim zestig keer zoveel tokens kunnen genereren als nu het geval is. Tokens zijn de basiseenheden die ai-modellen verwerken bij het genereren van tekst, afbeeldingen en andere output. De verwachte toename hangt samen met de verschuiving van ai als hulpmiddel naar systemen die continu actief zijn en steeds meer taken zelfstandig uitvoeren. Daardoor groeit niet alleen de vraag naar energie en processorkracht, maar ook naar efficiënere manieren om data op te slaan. Volgens Sandisk wordt opslag daarom een cruciale schakel in toekomstige ai-infrastructuur. items.title: Bij ABN AMRO bouwen developers aan technologie die ertoe doet
items.raw_text: Bij een bank denk je misschien niet direct aan cryptografie, AI-agents en complexe software engineering. Toch zijn dat precies de technische vraagstukken waar developers en cybersecurityspecialisten bij ABN AMRO dagelijks aan werken. Voor Benoît Viguier, cryptographer en software engineer bij de bank, betekent dit dat hij nieuwe technologie kan onderzoeken én oplossingen kan ontwikkelen die daadwerkelijk in de praktijk worden gebruikt. En dat binnen een IT-omgeving waarin betrouwbaarheid, veiligheid en schaalgrootte een belangrijke rol spelen. Benoît Viguier promoveerde aan de Radboud Universiteit en werkt sinds 2021 bij ABN AMRO. Hij houdt zich bezig met cryptografie, softwarebeveiliging en het ontwikkelen van tools waarmee andere developers veiliger kunnen werken. Wat hem aanspreekt, is de ruimte om te experimenteren en nieuwe ideeën uit te proberen. Tegelijkertijd weet hij dat zijn werk concrete resultaten moet opleveren. Want uiteindelijk moeten de oplossingen die hij ontwikkelt, bijdragen aan de veiligheid en betrouwbaarheid van de digitale dienstverlening van de bank. Technologie op grote schaal Banken in Nederland en Europa moderniseren hun IT-infrastructuur om voorbereid te zijn op toekomstige ontwikkelingen. items.title: Imec opent r&d-centrum in Finland en zet ook voet aan wal in Japan
items.raw_text: Imec opent een r&d-centrum in Espoo, Finland. Vorige week kondigde het Belgische onderzoekscentrum aan ook een lokaal team op te bouwen in Japan. Beide initiatieven draaien om fotonica, een technologie die volgens Imec cruciaal wordt om de datastromen van ai-systemen efficiënter te verwerken. Het team in Espoo ontwerpt, simuleert en test optische componenten en systemen. Het ontwikkelt ook demonstrators, werkende prototypes voor concrete toepassingen, op een hoger technologisch rijpheidsniveau. Zo wil Imec de kloof dichten tussen fotonische chiptechnologie en industriële toepassingen, zoals ai-infrastructuur, snelle communicatie en geavanceerde sensoren. Bij de opening waren de Vlaamse minister-president Matthias Diependaele en de Finse minister van Economische Zaken Sakari Puisto aanwezig. ‘Naarmate fotonica dieper doordringt in geavanceerde computersystemen, draait innovatie niet langer om snellere chips’, aldus Michael Peeters, vicepresident connected computing bij Imec. Hokkaido als eerste Japanse r&d-basis In Hokkaido werkt Imec met steun van het ministerie van Economie, Handel en Industrie (Meti) samen met het Leading-edge Semiconductor Technology Center (Lstc). Het team komt op de campus van de Hokkaido-universiteit in Sapporo en moet binnen vijf jaar groeien tot ongeveer vijftien onderzoekers en ingenieurs. items.title: Bedrijven massaal aan ai, maar baanbrekende innovatie blijft achter
items.raw_text: Bijna negen op de tien Nederlandse bedrijven gebruikt ai, maar de technologie leidt nog nauwelijks tot fundamenteel nieuwe producten en diensten. Dat blijkt uit de ‘Nederlandse Innovatie Monitor 2026’ van het Amsterdam Centre for Business Innovation (ACBI) van de Universiteit van Amsterdam en SEO Economisch Onderzoek . Bedrijven zetten ai vooral in voor tekstgeneratie en kantoorwerk. Zo gebruikt 68 procent van de organisaties grote taalmodellen voor tekstproductie. Fysieke toepassingen blijven vooralsnog achter. Ook verschilt de ai-volwassenheid per sector. Informatie en communicatie en de zakelijke en financiële dienstverlening lopen voorop, terwijl industrie, agro en energie achterblijven. Organisaties die ai effectief inzetten, presteren beter en innoveren meer. Vooral bedrijven die hun data en technologie op orde hebben, profiteren daarvan. Toch richten de meeste ondernemingen zich op verbetering van bestaande producten en diensten. De inspanningen op het gebied van radicale innovatie en managementinnovatie zijn dit jaar zelfs licht afgenomen. Volgens onderzoeksleider Henk Volberda, hoogleraar Strategie en Innovatie aan de UvA, is dat een gemiste kans. Efficiënter werken helpt de resultaten op korte termijn, maar is onvoldoende voor de toekomstige concurrentiekracht. items.title: Vacature: Beleidsmedewerker privacy en AI (GESLOTEN)
items.raw_text: We zoeken een beleidsmedewerker privacy en AI. Let op: deze vacature is gesloten en je kunt niet meer reageren. Over Bits of Freedom Bits of Freedom is een organisatie met grote ambities. We geloven dat een sterke democratische rechtsstaat nodig is om in vrijheid en gelijkheid samen te leven. De macht van technologie moet in handen zijn van de mensen die hier naar streven. In een digitale samenleving zijn het recht op privacy en communicatievrijheid essentieel om de macht van mensen te vergroten en dat van overheden en bedrijven te beknotten. Iedereen moet profiteren van de voordelen van het internet, en niemand mag de dupe worden van digitalisering. Dat gaat niet vanzelf. Met een team van ongeveer 19 bevlogen mensen, en vanuit een kantoor in Amsterdam, stellen we onrecht aan de kaak. We zijn professioneel en ambitieus. En met personeelsbeleid dat gelijke kansen stimuleert en bijdraagt aan het corrigeren van ongelijkheden in onze organisatie, netwerk en sector. items.title: Toezichthouder laat, ondanks veiligheidsrisico’s, gluurbrillen op de markt
items.raw_text: De Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP) zegt dat gluurbrillen ernstige risico's voor gebruikers en omstanders kunnen veroorzaken. Je zou denken dat de toezichthouder eist dat de brillen meteen worden teruggeroepen. Maar niets is minder waar. Vandaag publiceerde de Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP) haar onderzoek naar zes verschillende gluurbrillen. Uit het onderzoek blijkt dat deze niet alleen de privacy van omstanders in gevaar brengen, maar ook de veiligheid van gebruikers en mensen in hun omgeving. Deze risico’s beschouwt de AP als “zeer groot en ingrijpend”. Deze constatering volgt op een persbericht twee maanden eerder, waarin de toezichthouder stelde “dat filmen van anderen [met de gluurbril] vrijwel altijd verboden is.” Als je het ons vraagt, zijn de conclusies die de toezichthouder hieraan verbindt niet toereikend. De AP “raadt consumenten af om nu een [gluurbril] aan te schaffen” en roept fabrikanten op “relevante wetgeving beter mee te nemen in het ontwerp.” Maar voor product reviews gaan we wel naar Tweakers of de Consumentenbond, daar hebben we de Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens niet voor nodig. De AP heeft één heldere taak: het beschermen van burgers door onze privacywetgeving te handhaven. Dat vertikt ze. De gluurbril moet van de markt gehaald worden. Verbod We maken ons al langer zorgen over de zogenaamde gluurbrillen. Vorig jaar trokken we aan de bel over opticiens die de bril verkopen en riepen we de toezichthouder op om te handhaven voordat de brillen te ver genormal

items.title: We stellen graag aan je voor: Marlous van Wensveen!
items.raw_text: Marlous komt ons team versterken als Fondsenwerver donateurs & bedrijven. We stellen je graag aan haar voor. Daarnaast schuiven we onder het mom van veiligheid steeds verder op in de richting van een surveillancestaat. G renzen worden overschreden en dat is niet meer te rijmen met onze democratie . In je eentje is het soms lastig om zomaar iets te veranderen, maar met z’n allen kunnen we veel!
